extraction.name: MATHVISTA
extraction.description: A benchmark for evaluating mathematical reasoning of foundation models in visual contexts, consisting of 6,141 examples derived from 28 existing multimodal datasets and 3 newly created datasets.
extraction.creator: Pan Lu, Hritik Bansal, Tony Xia, Jiacheng Liu, Chunyuan Li, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Hao Cheng, Kai-Wei Chang, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was compiled by collecting 9 multimodal MathQA datasets, reviewing more than 70 VQA datasets and selecting 19 publicly available math-related ones using heuristic rules plus expert annotation, and creating 3 new datasets (IQTest, FunctionQA, PaperQA) with manual annotation and review.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Only 85.6% of examples have annotations because annotations were sourced from original data providers.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data came from 31 source datasets, including 28 existing multimodal datasets and 3 newly created datasets; IQTest was sourced from puzzle test figures on online learning platforms, and PaperQA used figures from papers released in August 2023 on Huggingface.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For VQA datasets, heuristic rules automatically selected examples likely involving mathematical reasoning by choosing examples with numeric answers or quantity words; false positives were then manually labeled, majority voting was used, each source dataset was capped at 400 examples, and testmini was created by random sampling with representation constraints.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Examples were annotated with metadata such as question type, answer type, language, source, category, task, grade level, and visual context from source dataset details. Three new datasets were manually annotated by graduate students in STEM fields and reviewed in a two-step process with three reviewers per dataset; VQA examples were manually labeled by three expert annotators for whether they involved mathematical reasoning; and 1,000 examples were manually labeled for mathematical reasoning categories.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Annotation quality was assessed using inter-annotation consistency, disagreement resolution by discussion, comparison of automatic versus human annotations, and Fleiss Kappa for mathematical reasoning labeling.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Graduate students in STEM fields; expert annotators; qualified human annotators with a high school diploma or higher for the human baseline.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The test answer labels will not be publicly released, an online evaluation platform will be maintained, and the authors are committed to maintaining the datasets, refining potential data noise, and evolving the leaderboard in response to community feedback and new models.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is intended to push AI assistants toward general-purpose capabilities and support development of AI agents for mathematically intensive and visually rich real-world tasks.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset may have bias from heterogeneous source annotations and sensitivity to demonstration bias in few-shot settings.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Limitations include incomplete coverage of mathematical problems and visuals, labor-intensive collection limiting scalability and generalizability, only 85.6% of examples having annotations, heterogeneous annotation formats, and focus on recent prominent models.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking and evaluation of foundation models for mathematical reasoning in visual contexts; testmini is intended for model development validation or limited compute, and test is for standard evaluation.

name.evidence: In this paper, we present M ATHVISTA , a consolidated Math ematical reasoning benchmark in Visual contexts.

description.evidence: To bridge this gap, we present M ATHVISTA , a benchmark designed to combine challenges from diverse mathematical and visual tasks. It consists of 6,141 examples, derived from 28 existing multimodal datasets involving mathematics and 3 newly created datasets ( i.e., IQTest, FunctionQA, and PaperQA).

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: Since these datasets are not originally math-targeted, we initially designed heuristic rules to automatically select examples likely to involve mathematical reasoning from a large pool of candidates. Examples with numeric answers or those containing quantity words (as listed in §D.1) in the questions were selected. This automatic filtration yielded 4,949 VQA-format examples, though some false positive examples remained. Therefore, we engaged three expert annotators to manually label these examples to determine if they involve mathematical reasoning... Utilizing majority voting and limiting each source dataset to 400 examples, we finalized a collection of 2,739 examples. To ensure that each source dataset is well represented in testmini and to maintain a distribution in testmini closely resembling the whole set, we adopted this sampling strategy: (1) first, randomly sample questions with a threshold number of 4 for each source dataset; (2) then, randomly sample the remaining questions for each source dataset on its proportion in the entire set.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: To facilitate fine-grained evaluation, examples are annotated with metadata, including question type, answer type, task category, grade level, visual context, and required reasoning skills. To ensure data quality, all questions were manually annotated by graduate students in STEM fields and further refined through a rigorous review process. To ensure consistency in annotation, we employed a two-step process. Initially, each dataset was independently annotated by three reviewers... Therefore, we engaged three expert annotators to manually label these examples to determine if they involve mathematical reasoning... To verify the quality of automatic annotation, expert annotators manually label the mathematical reasoning categories from seven candidates for 1,000 examples

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: Initially, each dataset was independently annotated by three reviewers, resulting in a high inter-annotation consistency rate of 99.2%. Specifically, among the newly collected 736 questions, only 6 exhibited disagreements in the annotated answers. Then, these discrepancies were resolved through discussion among the entire review team, ensuring a consensus was reached on each example. The results show that 94.1% of the examples from automatic and human annotations have the exact same set of reasoning types, while 98.79% of the individual labels are identical, indicating that the automatic annotation for the labeling of mathematical reasoning is highly accurate. Our analysis yielded a Fleiss Kappa score of 0.775, indicating a substantial level of consistency among the annotators.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: Our dataset, M ATHVISTA , is therefore motivated to bridge this gap, offering a robust evaluation benchmark for mathematical reasoning intertwined with visual understanding, thus pushing AI assistants towards general-purpose capabilities. This significant gap underscores the critical role that M ATHVISTA will play in the development of general-purpose AI agents capable of tackling mathematically intensive and visually rich real-world tasks.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Annotations were sourced from original data providers, resulting in only 85.6% of examples (Table 1) having annotations. Due to the heterogeneity of these sources, annotations lack a unified format and structure. In the question-only input setting (a), both Claude-2 and ChatGPT suffer from a performance drop, suggesting that they are more sensitive to the bias in demonstrations, especially in the absence of visual inputs.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: One limitation is the dataset coverage. While M ATHVISTA encompasses a broad spectrum of tasks and visual contexts, there may be gaps in the representation of certain types of mathematical problems and visuals. Furthermore, the dataset’s focus on mathematical reasoning within visual contexts, spanning specific domains like science and college-level math, necessitates a more labor-intensive process for collecting high-quality data compared to textual-only or general-purpose datasets. Thus, the scalability and generalizability of our benchmark to other domains remain a concem. rai:dataUseCases.evidence: Our goal is to conduct both qualitative and quantitative studies to provide a systematic evaluation of existing foundation models for mathematical reasoning capabilities in visual contexts using M ATHVISTA . MATHVISTA consists of 6,141 examples, divided into two subsets: testmini andtest.testmini contains 1,000 examples, intended for model development validation or for those with limited computing resources. The testset features the remaining 5,141 examples for standard evaluation.
